twoCoasts.metaTitle: Two coasts: which side of Thailand for your month
twoCoasts.metaDescription: Choose your month and see whether the Andaman coast or the Gulf of Thailand has the better weather, with our island picks for each side.
twoCoasts.title: Choose your month.
twoCoasts.intro: Thailand's two coasts have different monsoons. The southwest monsoon soaks the Andaman side from about May to October; the northeast monsoon brings the Gulf's heaviest rain from October to December. Pick a month and we'll show you which way to go.
twoCoasts.heroAlt: A beach on Thailand's Andaman coast
twoCoasts.andamanSub: Krabi, Railay, Koh Yao Noi, Koh Lanta, Phuket
twoCoasts.gulfSub: Koh Samui, Koh Phangan, Koh Kood

months.summary: The Andaman is in its best season: dry, calm and clear. The Gulf is drying out after its rains, with showers still possible early in the month.
months.andaman: Dry and sunny, calm sea. Peak season, so book early.
months.gulf: Mostly dry, with showers possible in the first weeks.
months.north: Cool, clear mornings. The best month for the north.

months.summary: Both coasts are good. The Andaman is dry and calm; the Gulf has entered its long dry season.
months.andaman: Dry, hot and calm. Excellent for sea canoeing.
months.gulf: Dry season begins. Good for Samui and Phangan.
months.north: Warm days, cool nights. Haze can start late in the month.

months.summary: Both coasts are dry and hot. A good month for either side, or for both.
months.north: Hot, and often hazy from agricultural burning.

months.summary: The hottest month. The Gulf is dry and calm; the Andaman is still good but the first storms can arrive late in the month.
months.andaman: Hot. Mostly dry, with the first storms possible.
months.north: The hottest and haziest month. We'd avoid it.

months.summary: The southwest monsoon reaches the Andaman coast. The Gulf stays mostly dry.
months.andaman: The rains begin. Rougher sea on west-facing beaches.
months.north: The first rains clear the air and green the hills.

months.summary: The Andaman is in its green season, with rough seas on exposed beaches. The Gulf is the beach for June.
months.andaman: Wet and windy. Some boats and hotels close.
months.north: Green and showery, with quiet temples.

months.summary: Summer holidays: go to the Gulf. The Andaman is green, quiet and often rough.
months.andaman: Wet, with rough sea on exposed coasts.
months.gulf: Good: mostly dry with occasional showers.

months.summary: Still the Gulf. The Andaman side has heavy rain and swells.
months.andaman: Wet, with swells on west-facing beaches.
months.gulf: Good: mostly dry with occasional showers.

months.summary: The wettest month on the Andaman side. The Gulf is still the better bet, though the rains are not far off.
months.andaman: Often the wettest month of the year.
months.gulf: Mixed, with more showers towards the end.
months.north: The wettest month in the north too.

months.summary: The awkward month. Early October, the Gulf is still drier; by late October the Andaman is drying out and the Gulf rains have begun.
months.andaman: Still wet, improving towards the end.
months.gulf: Fine early in the month, then the northeast monsoon arrives.
months.north: The rains ease. Green, fresh and quiet.

months.summary: Go west. The Andaman is drying out and the Gulf has its wettest weeks.
months.andaman: Drying out; the season starts again.
months.gulf: The wettest month on Samui and Phangan.

months.summary: The Andaman is dry and calm. The Gulf is still in its rains.
months.gulf: Rain likely, especially early in the month.

twoCoasts.koodNote: Koh Kood, in the far east of the Gulf, follows the Andaman's pattern more than Samui's: it is best from November to April.
twoCoasts.tableNote: Based on long-term patterns. Weather varies from year to year; this is not a forecast.
twoCoasts.sources: We check these patterns against the Thai Meteorological Department's climate data before each season.

khlongs.metaTitle: Bangkok khlong map: the canals of Thonburi by longtail
khlongs.metaDescription: A living map of Bangkok's canals: two longtail routes through the khlongs of Thonburi, with the stops, the times and the tide.
khlongs.title: Bangkok from the khlong.
khlongs.intro: Before roads, Bangkok's streets were water. On the Thonburi bank the khlongs are still lived on. These are the two routes we use most, drawn as the water runs.
khlongs.heroAlt: Wooden houses on stilts along a Thonburi canal
khlongs.mapLabel: Schematic map of the Chao Phraya river and the Thonburi canals, with two longtail routes

routes.name: Route A: The morning loop
routes.text: From Tha Tien pier across the river into Khlong Bangkok Yai, through Khlong Bang Luang and back by Wat Arun. Our usual first morning in Bangkok.

routes.name: Route B: The long way north
routes.text: Up the river to Khlong Bangkok Noi and the Royal Barges, through orchards and quieter canals to Taling Chan, and back down Khlong Bangkok Yai.

stops.name: Tha Tien pier
stops.text: Where we meet. Wat Pho is behind you, Wat Arun across the water.

stops.name: Wat Arun
stops.text: The Temple of Dawn, seen from the river as the light comes up.

stops.name: Khlong Bangkok Yai
stops.text: The wide canal into Thonburi: wooden houses, temple landings and morning cooking.

stops.name: Khlong Bang Luang
stops.text: An old wooden house where artists work and the boat stops for coffee.

stops.name: Wat Paknam Phasi Charoen
stops.text: A great white stupa above the canal, visible from far along the water.

stops.name: Royal Barges Museum
stops.text: The long carved barges used for royal processions on the river.

stops.name: Khlong Bangkok Noi
stops.text: Quieter water, temples and gardens as the city thins out.

stops.name: Taling Chan
stops.text: Orchards and, at weekends, a floating market where the locals shop.

khlongs.tide: The khlongs rise and fall with the river. At very high water some low bridges are hard to pass; at very low water the smaller canals are too shallow. Your boatman reads the water and adjusts the route on the day.

practical.title: When
practical.text: Early morning, all year. From September to November the river runs high; we check the conditions every day.

practical.title: The boat
practical.text: A private longtail with a licensed boatman and life jackets for everyone, children's sizes included.

practical.title: Respect
practical.text: These are people's homes. Wave, don't point the camera into windows, and keep voices low near the temples.

responsible.metaTitle: Elephants and hill tribes: how we travel responsibly in Thailand
responsible.metaDescription: How to choose an ethical elephant sanctuary in Thailand and visit hill-tribe villages respectfully: what Longtail Travel books, what it doesn't, and why.
responsible.title: Watched, not ridden.
responsible.intro: Elephants and hill-tribe villages are part of many trips to northern Thailand, and both are easy to get wrong. This is how we choose, and how we ask our travellers to behave.
responsible.heroAlt: Wild elephants in a Thai national park
responsible.elephantsText: Thailand has thousands of captive elephants, many of them in tourism. Riding, bathing, shows and painting all depend on training and control that harm the animals. A good sanctuary lets elephants behave like elephants, and you watch.
weBookList: Observation-based sanctuaries, where you watch from a distance
Small groups, with time limits around the animals
Places that are open about how many elephants they keep and where they came from
Wild elephants in national parks, with a park guide and from a vehicle or hide
weDontList: Riding, with or without a saddle
Baby elephants kept for visitors to handle
responsible.checklistText: Before we add a sanctuary, we ask these questions. You can ask them too.

checklist.title: Can the elephants roam?
checklist.text: Look for space, forest and grazing, and herds that choose where they go during the day.

checklist.title: Is there any contact?
checklist.text: If the visit includes riding, bathing or close feeding, it is not a sanctuary in our sense.

checklist.title: Are hooks or chains in use?
checklist.text: Bullhooks and short chains are signs of control, not care.

checklist.title: How many visitors?
checklist.text: Small, timed groups and quiet days off for the herd.

checklist.title: Is there a vet?
checklist.text: Ask about veterinary care, diet and the elephants' histories.

checklist.title: What do independent welfare groups say?
checklist.text: We follow the guidance of animal-welfare organisations and look for places that welcome scrutiny.

responsible.tribesText: The hills of the north are home to many peoples, among them the Karen, Hmong, Akha, Lahu, Lisu and Mien. A visit can be a real exchange, or it can feel like walking through someone's home with a camera.

tribesList.title: Go with someone from the community
tribesList.text: We use guides from the village or community-run projects, so the visit is invited and the money stays there.

tribesList.title: Ask before you photograph
tribesList.text: Always ask, and accept a no. Never photograph inside a home or a ceremony without permission.

tribesList.title: Dress and behave as a guest
tribesList.text: Cover shoulders and knees, take shoes off where others do, and don't touch spirit gates or shrines.

tribesList.title: Buy directly, pay fairly
tribesList.text: Buy crafts from the makers. Don't hand out sweets or money to children.

tribesList.title: No human zoos
tribesList.text: We don't book villages where Kayan women with brass neck-rings are presented as an attraction.

faq.a: It is often sold that way, but it means close contact with animals that have to be controlled to allow it. We prefer to watch elephants bathe themselves.
Yes, in some national parks, such as Khao Yai and Kui Buri, with a park guide. Sightings are never guaranteed.

faq.q: Will we be able to buy crafts?
faq.a: Yes, and we encourage it, directly from the people who make them.

responsible.sources: For independent guidance on wildlife tourism, see the advice published by World Animal Protection.
